## The X axis should be "1-Specificity" instead of "Specificity"!

This is not a bug! 

Most statistical tools cannot plot specificity from 1 to 0, so instead they plot
1-specificity from 0 to 1. This results in exactly the same plot, just with a
different labelling of the axis.

R doesn't have this limitation, and `pROC` plots specificity from 1 to 0, saving
you from doing a few subtractions when you look at the plot.

If you are concerned that your reviewers will be confused and really wish to
have the "old-style" 1-Specificity from 0 to 1, or if you plan to change the
axis label to "False Positive Rate" (which is really 1-specificity), you can use
the `legacy.axes` argument to the plot function. See `?plot.roc` for more
details.

Here is a comparison of the two plotting styles:

```{r legacy-axis-comparison, fig.width=10, fig.height=5, fig.align='center', out.width='100%', message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(pROC)
data(aSAH)

# Create a ROC curve
rocobj <- roc(aSAH$outcome, aSAH$s100b)

# Plot with default axis (Specificity from 1 to 0)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(rocobj, main = "Default: Specificity (1 to 0)")

# Plot with legacy axis (1-Specificity from 0 to 1)
plot(rocobj, main = "Legacy: 1-Specificity (0 to 1)", 
     legacy.axes = TRUE)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

## I have a GLM/SVM/PLS/<INSERT YOUR FAVORITE MODEL HERE> model, how can I analyze it with pROC?

You need to use the `predict()` function to get predictions that can be passed
to pROC (as the `predictor` argument).

Specifically you need to get a single vector of numeric predictions. In some
cases you may have to add pass `type="probabilities"` or something similar to
the `predict` function (to get probabilities instead of the binary response),
sometimes you may to have select one of the column of the returned matrix (if
`predict` returns a matrix of class probabilities). Read the documentation of
the package you're using and look at your results to find out what to do
exactly.

Here is a concrete example using `glm()`:

```{r glm-example, fig.width=5, fig.height=5, fig.align='center', message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Fit a logistic regression model
model <- glm(outcome ~ s100b + wfns, data = aSAH, family = binomial)

# Get predicted probabilities
predictions <- predict(model, type = "response")

# Create ROC curve with the predictions
roc_glm <- roc(aSAH$outcome, predictions)

# Plot and compute AUC
plot(roc_glm, main = "ROC curve from GLM predictions")
auc(roc_glm)
```

## How do I remove empty space on the sides of my ROC plot?

Extra empty space can sometimes appear on either side of the x-axis in your ROC plots.
This typically happens when the plotting device or window isn't square. By default, pROC
ensures the plot is square (with `asp = 1`) so that both sensitivity and specificity are
on the same scale, which is important for visual interpretation.

```{r default-empty-space, fig.width=7, fig.height=5, fig.align='center', message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
rocobj <- roc(aSAH$outcome, aSAH$s100b, percent = TRUE)
plot(rocobj, main = "Default ROC plot (non-squared, with empty space)")
```

### Solution 1: Make the plotting region square

Use `par(pty = "s")` to make the plotting region square, which will automatically
remove the extra space:

```{r remove-empty-space, fig.width=7, fig.height=5, fig.align='center', message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
par(pty = "s")
rocobj <- roc(aSAH$outcome, aSAH$s100b, percent = TRUE)
plot(rocobj, main = "ROC curve with square plotting region")
par(pty = "m")  # Reset to default
```

### Solution 2: Adjust margins for square device

If you're saving to a file, make sure the device is square and adjust margins so
that top + bottom == left + right:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# For file output
png("roc.png", width = 480, height = 480)
par(mar = c(4, 4, 4, 4) + 0.1)
plot(roc(aSAH$outcome, aSAH$s100b, percent = TRUE))
dev.off()
```

### Solution 3: Allow free aspect ratio (not recommended)

You can use `asp = NA` to allow a free (unconstrained) aspect ratio, but this will
distort the axis and make visual interpretation of the ROC curve difficult. It's
better to keep the plot square for proper visual comparison.

```{r free-aspect-ratio, fig.width=7, fig.height=5, fig.align='center', message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
rocobj <- roc(aSAH$outcome, aSAH$s100b, percent = TRUE)
plot(rocobj, main = "ROC curve with free aspect ratio", asp = NA)
```

**Note:** Having a squared ROC curve is important for visual interpretation, as it
allows you to compare distances to the diagonal accurately. The default `asp = 1`
in `plot.roc()` (and `coord_fixed()` in `ggroc()`) enforces this. To drop the
fixed aspect ratio on a ggplot, replace the coord:
`ggroc(rocobj) + coord_cartesian()`.

## When I resample or randomize my dataset I get an biased AUC > 0.5. How come?

This is because pROC tries to auto-detect the direction of the decision due to
the default value of `direction="auto"`. The decision is based on the median of
the groups instead of the AUC directly, so you the effect may not be 1:1, but
you should expect to obtain AUC > 0.5 on average.

Whenever you are resampling with pROC you need to explicitly pass an explicit
value to `direction`, either `direction="<"` or `direction=">"`. I also
recommend taking a minute to set the `levels` (value of the `response` for
controls and cases, respectively) argument explicitly too.

pROC prints a message such as `Setting direction: controls < cases` when it
auto-detects the direction (unless `quiet = TRUE`).

## Can I test if a single ROC curve is significantly different from 0.5?

Yes, with `roc.test(roc1)`: without a second curve, it tests the (partial) AUC
against the absence of discrimination, with the DeLong, ML or bootstrap
variance.

The AUC is the probability that a randomly chosen case has a higher value than a
randomly chosen control (counting ties as 1/2). The [Wilcoxon Rank Sum
Test](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/stats/topics/wilcox.test) (also
known as the Mann-Whitney U test) is the usual alternative: its statistic `W`
divided by the number of case-control pairs is the AUC (Hanley and McNeil, 1982).
Note that its null hypothesis is that cases and controls have the same
distribution. That implies an AUC of 0.5, but not the reverse: with different
spreads, it can reject even when the AUC is 0.5. It is not a test of the medians
either, which can be identical even when the AUC is far from 0.5.

## My dataset is huge. Can I use pROC?

A large effort has been made to render pROC more and more efficient with large
ROC curves. An algorithm with complexity of O(n) has been rolled out with pROC
1.6 and improved over time. Improvements to the DeLong test and the `coords`
functions have been implemented too.

If you feel that a function is abnormally slow, especially in comparison to
other packages, feel free to [open a bug
report](https://github.com/xrobin/pROC/issues/new?template=Bug_report.md).

## Can I compute the confidence interval of the best threshold of the curve (not its SE/SP)?

Yes you can since pROC 1.6 and its `ci.coords` function. For instance:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
ci.coords(aSAH$outcome, aSAH$s100b, x="best", input = "threshold",
          ret="threshold")
# 95% CI (2000 stratified bootstrap replicates):
#  threshold threshold.low threshold.median threshold.high
#       best         0.155            0.205          0.485
```

The 95% bootstrap confidence interval of the optimal threshold is 0.155-0.485.

## How do I get the best threshold, or a threshold for a given sensitivity?

`coords()` with `x = "best"` returns the threshold that maximizes the Youden
index (or minimizes the distance to the top-left corner with
`best.method = "closest.topleft"`). `best.weights` sets the cost of false
negatives and the prevalence.

```{r}
library(pROC)
data(aSAH)
r.s100b <- roc(aSAH$outcome, aSAH$s100b, quiet = TRUE)
coords(r.s100b, "best")
```

To find the threshold with the highest specificity under a minimum sensitivity,
list all the thresholds and filter them:

```{r}
all.coords <- coords(r.s100b, "all", ret = c("threshold", "sensitivity", "specificity"),
                     transpose = FALSE)
eligible <- all.coords[all.coords$sensitivity >= 0.75, ]
eligible[which.max(eligible$specificity), ]
```

Asking `coords(r.s100b, 0.75, input = "sensitivity")` instead gives the
specificity at a sensitivity of exactly 0.75, interpolated on the curve. No
threshold produces that point, so the `threshold` is `NA`. In the other
direction, `coords(r.s100b, 0.2, input = "threshold", ret = c("sensitivity", "specificity"))`
gives the sensitivity and specificity of a given threshold. See the previous
question for a confidence interval.

## How do I compare two ROC curves or AUCs?

Use `roc.test()`. By default it detects whether the curves are paired (built
from the same patients, in the same order) and prints it with `Setting paired`.
The choice matters, and you can set it with `paired = TRUE` or `paired = FALSE`:

```{r}
r.ndka <- roc(aSAH$outcome, aSAH$ndka, quiet = TRUE)
roc.test(r.s100b, r.ndka, paired = TRUE)$p.value
roc.test(r.s100b, r.ndka, paired = FALSE)$p.value
```

The default method for the AUC is DeLong's; `method = "bootstrap"` is
available too. Partial AUCs are compared by the bootstrap test, with the
`partial.auc` arguments (see the question on partial AUC below).

## How do I set which group is the cases, and what does `direction` do?

`roc()` needs to know which values of the response are the controls and the
cases (`levels = c(control, case)`), and whether the predictor is higher in
cases (`direction = "<"`) or in controls (`direction = ">"`). If you don't
set them, pROC makes a guess and tells you with `Setting levels` and
`Setting direction`:

```{r}
roc(aSAH$outcome, aSAH$s100b)$levels
```

With more than two levels, pROC takes the first two (and warns): use `levels`,
or `multiclass.roc()`.

The `direction = "auto"` default picks the direction from the group medians,
so the curve usually ends up above the diagonal. That hides a reversed `levels`
or a predictor that goes the other way:

```{r}
auc(roc(aSAH$outcome, aSAH$s100b, levels = c("Poor", "Good"), quiet = TRUE))
auc(roc(aSAH$outcome, aSAH$s100b, levels = c("Poor", "Good"), direction = "<", quiet = TRUE))
```

In the second call, the AUC is 1 minus the first one: the controls are the
"Poor" outcomes and the predictor is higher in the other group. Set both
arguments explicitly whenever the result will be used in code, and always when
you resample (see above).

## Why do I get "Predictor must be numeric or ordered" or "Response and predictor must be vectors of the same length"?

The predictor must be numeric or an ordered factor. A character vector or an
unordered factor, such as a predicted class label, triggers the first message.
Pass a score (a probability, a numeric predictor) or convert an ordinal
predictor with `factor(x, ordered = TRUE)`.

The second message means that the response and the predictor have a different
number of observations. A common cause is a model fitted with `glm()` or `lm()`
on data with missing values: the model silently drops the incomplete rows,
and `predict()` returns fewer values than the response has. Either remove the
incomplete rows before fitting, or use the response stored in the model
(`model$y` for `glm`).

## Why does another package, or caret, give a different AUC?

On the same scores, `ROCR` gives the same AUC as pROC, including when the
predictor has many ties. The differences come from the input and the way the
AUC is aggregated:

* **Direction.** ROCR assumes that higher values mean cases, while pROC detects
  the direction. If the predictor is higher in controls, ROCR gives 1 - AUC,
  which pROC reproduces with `direction = "<"`.
* **Scores or classes.** The AUC of predicted classes (0/1) is not the AUC of the
  scores they come from. For a logistic regression on `aSAH`, the AUC of the
  probabilities is 0.775, and that of the thresholded 0/1 classes is 0.687.
  Use the probabilities (`type = "response"`).
* **Cross-validation.** The AUC computed on all the cross-validated predictions
  pooled together is not the mean of the AUC of each fold. On a 5-fold
  cross-validation of the same model we got 0.747 pooled and 0.773 averaged.
  caret's `twoClassSummary` reports the mean of the per-fold AUCs, which you can
  reproduce with pROC on each `Resample` of the saved predictions.

## How do I plot several ROC curves, with confidence intervals?

Put the curves in a list and give it to `ggroc()`, or draw them one after the
other with `lines()` or `add = TRUE`:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
r.wfns <- roc(aSAH$outcome, aSAH$wfns, quiet = TRUE)
ggroc(list(s100b = r.s100b, ndka = r.ndka, wfns = r.wfns))

plot(r.s100b)
lines(r.ndka, col = "red")
```

Confidence intervals of the sensitivity at given specificities are drawn on
top of a curve with `ci.se()` and `plot()`:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
plot(r.s100b)
plot(ci.se(r.s100b, specificities = seq(0, 1, 0.05)), type = "shape")
```

The `ggplot2` vignette (`vignette("ggroc")`) shows the options of `ggroc()`,
including the diagonal and the 1-specificity axis.

## How do I compute a partial AUC?

Give the `partial.auc` interval (on the scale of the curve) to `auc()` or
`roc()`. By default it is an interval of specificity, `partial.auc.focus =
"sensitivity"` switches it, and `partial.auc.correct = TRUE` applies the
McClish standardization, so that 0.5 is no discrimination and 1 a perfect curve:

```{r}
auc(r.s100b, partial.auc = c(1, 0.8))
auc(r.s100b, partial.auc = c(1, 0.8), partial.auc.correct = TRUE)
auc(r.s100b, partial.auc = c(1, 0.8), partial.auc.focus = "sensitivity")
```

On a curve with `percent = TRUE` the interval is in percent (`c(100, 80)`); on
a curve in fractions, `auc()` refuses `c(100, 80)`. The confidence interval and the comparison of partial AUCs
use the bootstrap.

## The functions are giving me weird error messages I don't understand

Several packages on CRAN provide alternative `roc` or `auc` functions. These
packages can interfere with pROC, especially if they are loaded later in the
session (and hence appear earlier in the search path).

For instance, here are a few messages you may see if you have the `AUC` package loaded:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
roc(outcome ~ ndka, data = aSAH)
# Not enough distinct predictions to compute area under the ROC curve.
# 
# Error in roc(outcome ~ ndka, data = aSAH) : unused argument (data = aSAH)
```

If that happens, you should unload the package by typing `detach("package:AUC")`.
To find out where the function is coming from, simply type its name on the R
prompt:

```r
roc
```

The line at the bottom indicates that the function comes from the AUC package.

In addition, you may have defined a `roc` function yourself. In this case,
`rm(roc)` will solve the problem.

Alternatively you can refer to the pROC version of the function specifically
through their namespace:

```r
pROC::auc(pROC::roc(aSAH$outcome, aSAH$ndka))
```

Here is a list of packages providing `roc`, `auc` and `ci` functions which will
hide pROC's functions if the package is loaded after pROC:
